title: Beauty and charm jet identification with end-to-end training on a superconducting quantum processor
authors: Lucio Anderlini, Pietro Asinari, Gianluca Bertaina, Davide Calonico, Marco Coïsson, Alessio Gianelle
abstract: The identification of heavy-flavor jets, i.e. collimated streams of particles originating from the fragmentation of beauty and charm quarks produced in proton-proton collisions, represents one of the most challenging classification tasks in measurements at Large Hadron Collider experiments. In recent years, advanced machine learning techniques have been successfully employed to address this problem, while quantum machine learning has emerged as a promising alternative approach. However, the high dimensionality of the problem, typically involving hundreds of observables, raises an open question: whether the current generation of quantum computers, characterized by limited qubit count, can effectively tackle such complex tasks. In this work, a variational quantum circuit for the classification of b- and c-jets at the LHCb experiment is implemented on a 5-qubit superconducting quantum computer manufactured by IQM and installed at the Politecnico di Torino. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of a quantum algorithm for jet identification using simulated data from an LHC experiment in which all stages of the machine-learning workflow, including training and testing, are performed on real quantum hardware. The results demonstrate that the impact of hardware-induced quantum noise does not significantly degrade the performance. A framework for the evaluation of the training time on the quantum hardware and for the circuit optimization is also proposed. These findings pave the way for future applications on larger quantum devices based on superconducting qubits, featuring a larger number of qubits enabling the encoding of information beyond the reach of classical simulation and providing a step toward investigating whether quantum advantage may eventually be achievable in high-energy physics classification tasks.

infographic.key_insight: A 5-qubit superconducting processor demonstrated end-to-end quantum training and testing for beauty-versus-charm jet identification without significant performance degradation from hardware noise.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The work demonstrates a real-hardware classification workflow and proposes a framework for estimating training time and optimizing circuits on resource-limited quantum processors.
method: Classify simulated LHCb beauty and charm jets using a variational quantum circuit.
Perform both training and testing on an IQM 5-qubit superconducting processor at Politecnico di Torino.
Evaluate hardware-noise effects and develop a training-time and circuit-optimization framework.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation on simulated LHCb collision data found that hardware-induced quantum noise did not significantly degrade classification performance; the abstract provides no numerical metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Quantum advantage remains unproven, and scaling to high-dimensional jet data on larger devices requires further investigation.
infographic.paper_title: Beauty and charm jet identification with end-to-end training on a superconducting quantum processor

title: Programming Quantum Circuit Parameters with Large Language Models
authors: Tiago de Souza Farias, Caio Moraes Porto, Matheus da Silva Fonseca, Nicolas Armando Cabrera Carpi, Anderson de Araujo Oliveira, Celso Jorge Villas-Boas
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently demonstrated the ability to generate parameters for variational quantum circuits without conventional optimization. However, the conditions under which this approach is effective remain unclear. Here, we investigate a frozen, general-purpose LLM that generates complete circuit parameter vectors from symbolic circuit and Hamiltonian descriptions, with optional iterative energy feedback. We evaluate the approach on general random Hamiltonians, structured parent Hamiltonians, and molecular systems. For general Hamiltonians, LLM-generated parameters exhibit larger energy errors than conventional Adam optimization, while additional feedback generally provides limited improvement. In contrast, for structured Hamiltonians, the LLM can generate promising low-energy parameter configurations, suggesting that identifiable physical and mathematical structure facilitates parameter inference. We also show that direct LLM predictions of minimum energies can violate the Hamiltonian spectral lower bound, whereas generated circuit parameters allow independent evaluation of physically realizable energy expectation values. Finally, we investigate blind circuit interpretation and find that the LLM can predict measurement outcomes even when it fails to identify the underlying quantum algorithm. These findings highlight the role of problem structure, the limitations of iterative LLM optimization, and the importance of independently verifiable predictions in quantum parameter programming.

infographic.key_insight: A frozen, general-purpose LLM can propose low-energy quantum circuit parameters for structured problems, but performs worse than Adam optimization on general random Hamiltonians.
infographic.engineering_relevance: LLM-generated circuit parameters offer independently evaluable candidates, making them more reliable to assess than direct, potentially unphysical energy predictions.
method: Generate complete circuit parameter vectors from symbolic circuit and Hamiltonian descriptions.
Optionally refine parameters using iterative energy feedback.
Evaluate random, structured parent, and molecular Hamiltonians, plus blind circuit interpretation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluations found larger energy errors than Adam on general Hamiltonians, limited gains from feedback, and promising low-energy configurations for structured Hamiltonians.
infographic.watch_item: Do not assume physical validity of direct minimum-energy predictions: some fell below the Hamiltonian spectral lower bound.
infographic.paper_title: Programming Quantum Circuit Parameters with Large Language Models

title: Multi-head Quantum Neural Networks: Replacing Transformer Blocks with NISQ Modules inside a 30-Billion-Parameter LLM
authors: Maforikan Amoussou, Borja Aizpurua, Sukhbinder Singh, Román Orús, Hans-Arno Jacobsen
abstract: We introduce the multi-head quantum neural network (QNN), a quantum module compatible with noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices that can replace transformer blocks inside pre-trained large language models (LLMs) with little loss in accuracy and with far fewer parameters than the blocks it replaces. Encoding a model's $D$ hidden neurons into a qubit register is the obstacle: amplitude encoding scales poorly in circuit depth and angle encoding in qubit count, so neither is practical at production-scale width. We instead partition the hidden space into $k$ disjoint heads, angle-encode each into an $n_q$-qubit register, process the heads in parallel, and couple them through constrained classical linear layers, the mixers. Performing surgery on Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, we show that a single multi-head QNN with $145\,281$ trainable parameters ($D=2048$, $k=32$, $n_q=8$, $L=4$) can replace a contiguous span of eight transformer blocks, displacing $16.33\%$ of the model's parameters. Ablations show that, for a single replaced block, the quantum heads (circuits followed by a learned readout), and not the classical mixers alone, recover the displaced function, whereas for fused spans the mixers alone come within $1$-$3\%$ of the full module in perplexity. Whether this benefit is specific to trained, entangling quantum circuits is not established: controls that switch the entangler off (two seeds), or freeze the circuit at its initial or at uniformly random angles (one seed), beat the full module on held-out perplexity, and a parameter-matched classical multilayer perceptron remains a few percent ahead of the full module. We train classically with exact statevector simulation, then execute the quantum heads of our fusion checkpoints on a $156$-qubit IBM Heron processor, showing that NISQ-scale quantum modules can be installed in a production-scale LLM and run on hardware.

infographic.key_insight: A 145,281-parameter multi-head quantum module replaced eight contiguous transformer blocks in a 30-billion-parameter LLM, displacing 16.33% of its parameters.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Partitioning hidden states into small quantum heads enables NISQ-compatible integration into production-scale LLM architectures without encoding the entire hidden space at once.
method: Partition 2,048 hidden dimensions into 32 heads, each angle-encoded on 8 qubits.
Process heads with depth-L=4 quantum circuits and learned readouts, coupled through constrained classical mixers.
Train using exact statevector simulation, then execute fusion-checkpoint quantum heads on a 156-qubit IBM Heron processor.
infographic.evidence_signal: Held-out perplexity ablations found mixer-only fused modules within 1–3% of the full module, while a parameter-matched classical MLP remained a few percent better.
infographic.watch_item: Quantum advantage is not established: limited-seed non-entangling and frozen-circuit controls outperformed the full module, and training used classical simulation.
infographic.paper_title: Multi-head Quantum Neural Networks: Replacing Transformer Blocks with NISQ Modules inside a 30-Billion-Parameter LLM

title: A Unified Benchmarking Study of Variational Quantum Eigensolver Ansatz for Electronic Structure Problems
authors: Julie Maria Raju, Abhoy Kole, Julen Larrucea, Kamalika Datta, Lennart Weingarten, Rolf Drechsler
abstract: Electronic structure calculations become computationally expensive on classical computers as electron correlation increases. Quantum computing offers a promising alternative through hybrid quantum-classical Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) on Noisy-Intermediate Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices. The choice of ansatz plays a pivotal role in the performance and scalability of the VQE, yet selecting an optimal ansatz remains challenging. Existing approaches including chemically inspired ansatz, adaptive schemes and Hardware Efficient Ansätze (HEA) lack a unified comparison. This gap makes the scalability and trade-offs of each method unclear for varying molecular sizes. This work presents a systematic benchmarking study comparing Unitary Couples Cluster Singles and Doubles Ansatz (UCCSD), fermionic ADAPT-VQE, BasicPCA HEA, and Excitation Preserving HEA across molecules of varying size like $H_2$, $LiH$, $N_2$. We evaluate trade-offs among circuit depth, parameter count, ground-state energy error, and NISQ feasibility. ADAPT-VQE achieves accuracy comparable to UCCSD with lower resource overhead, but becomes impractical for modest system sizes ($\sim$10 electrons) due to increasing circuit complexity. In contrast, HEA reduces hardware costs but requires more parameters and sacrifices accuracy, with performance strongly dependent on molecular size. The Excitation Preserving ansatz remains below chemical accuracy for $H_2$ and $LiH$, and fails for $N_2$, underscoring the need to balance expressibility and trainability. Overall, these results highlight key trade-offs between accuracy and resource efficiency across VQE ansätze, emphasizing the need to improve ADAPT-VQE scalability and HEA accuracy while addressing optimization challenges for near-term quantum hardware.

infographic.key_insight: VQE benchmarking reveals an accuracy–resource trade-off: ADAPT-VQE approaches UCCSD accuracy with lower overhead, while hardware-efficient ansätze reduce hardware costs but sacrifice accuracy.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Choosing a VQE ansatz for near-term quantum hardware requires balancing circuit depth, parameter count, molecular size, and optimization difficulty.
method: Compare UCCSD, fermionic ADAPT-VQE, BasicPCA, and Excitation Preserving ansätze.
Benchmark electronic structure calculations for H₂, LiH, and N₂.
Evaluate ground-state energy error, circuit depth, parameter count, and NISQ feasibility.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across the tested molecules, ADAPT-VQE delivers accuracy comparable to UCCSD, but its circuit complexity becomes impractical around 10 electrons; hardware-efficient performance depends strongly on molecular size.
infographic.watch_item: Lower hardware cost does not guarantee useful accuracy: the Excitation Preserving ansatz fails for N₂, highlighting expressibility and trainability concerns.
infographic.paper_title: A Unified Benchmarking Study of Variational Quantum Eigensolver Ansatz for Electronic Structure Problems

title: Hierarchical Decoding for Quantum Error Correction
authors: Xulong Tang, Narges Alavisamani, Joan Camps, Matthew Cha, Elise Jennings, Jack O'Connor
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires classical decoders that can keep up with syndrome data streams and supply correction information and logical measurement outcomes to the quantum control system. Meeting these requirements at scale requires high throughput while controlling the end-to-end latency from readout to usable correction. In this paper, we organize decoding algorithms, execution strategies, and code constructions using common classifications and examine their performance and trade-offs under the reported evaluation conditions. We distinguish decoder-level hierarchy, where multiple decoding stages or resources cooperate to decode a single code, from code-level hierarchy, where the code construction itself introduces multiple decoding levels. We first review single-code hierarchical decoders and their cascaded predecoding and windowed, streaming, and distributed implementations. We then study hierarchical and concatenated codes, focusing on how decoding is coordinated across code levels through hard decisions, soft reliability information, or syndrome information. We also examine how qubit modalities shape decoding workloads and timing requirements, and review how different decoding platforms meet these requirements, including central processing units (CPUs), graphics processing units (GPUs), field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs), application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs), and cryogenic platforms. By assessing design trade-offs, this paper clarifies connections across the literature and provides a shared foundation for QEC design exploration. It also identifies gaps in performance reporting and system integration to guide future research toward practical quantum error correction.

infographic.key_insight: Hierarchical quantum error correction spans both cooperating decoder stages and multilevel code constructions, with distinct throughput, latency, and coordination trade-offs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Practical fault-tolerant systems must match decoder architecture and hardware to syndrome workloads and end-to-end correction deadlines.
method: Classify decoder-level and code-level hierarchy.
Review cascaded, windowed, streaming, and distributed decoding.
Compare cross-level information exchange and CPU, GPU, FPGA, ASIC, and cryogenic platforms.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes a literature-based comparison under reported evaluation conditions, without presenting numerical benchmarks or a new experimental validation.
infographic.watch_item: Gaps in performance reporting and system integration limit direct comparisons and confidence in deployment readiness.
infographic.paper_title: Hierarchical Decoding for Quantum Error Correction

title: Infinite or indefinite: the query cost of simulating the quantum switch
authors: Dantong Li
abstract: The quantum switch applies two operations in a coherent superposition of their causal orders and is a simple example of indefinite causal order. No quantum circuit that uses each operation once in a definite order can even describe it, yet photonic experiments have demonstrated its physical realization. We ask how many calls to the black-box operations a quantum computer in the circuit model needs to reproduce the switch. If one of the black boxes is known to be unitary, three calls suffice. For general channels on a $d$-dimensional system, we prove three results. In all three, circuits may use classical feed-forward and unlimited ancillary quantum memory. First, no finite number of calls suffices for exact simulation in the worst case. Second, approximation to any fixed error below $1/2$, measured in half the diamond norm, requires $Ω(d^{1/4})$ calls, exponential in the number of qubits. Third, an ordinary circuit can require exponentially many calls to obtain a single bit that the switch extracts with a few uses. We consider a device whose actual noise is dephasing in a fixed unknown basis and test it against a theoretical depolarizing model. The two channels have the same entanglement and average gate fidelities, so these figures alone do not distinguish them. At fixed noise strength, the quantum switch tells them apart with a number of device uses independent of $d$, whereas the circuit model requires $Ω(d^{1/16})$ calls. Noise characterization is needed for quantum error correction, and this gives a provable query advantage of the switch in a task relevant to practical quantum computing. We invite future work that extends such advantages to more practical computing tasks.

infographic.key_insight: The quantum switch offers provable query advantages over definite-order circuits: exact simulation of general channels is impossible with finitely many calls in the worst case.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For noise characterization relevant to quantum error correction, the switch can distinguish channels with identical entanglement and average gate fidelities using far fewer device calls.
method: Compare coherent superpositions of operation orders with definite-order circuits allowing classical feed-forward and unlimited ancillary memory.
Prove query lower bounds for exact and approximate simulation of general d-dimensional channels.
Analyze discrimination of dephasing in a fixed unknown basis from a theoretical depolarizing model.
infographic.evidence_signal: Theoretical bounds show Ω(d^{1/4}) calls for simulation at fixed half-diamond-norm error below 1/2, and Ω(d^{1/16}) circuit calls for noise discrimination versus dimension-independent switch usage at fixed noise strength.
infographic.watch_item: These are theoretical query advantages; practical benefits depend on implementing the switch reliably and extending the results to realistic computing tasks.
infographic.paper_title: Infinite or indefinite: the query cost of simulating the quantum switch

title: Hybrid Classical-Quantum Optimization for CVRPTW: A Systems Framework with Provable Feasibility and Empirical Hardware Limits
authors: Syamasundar Gopasana, Swatantra Singh, Rohan Joydhar, Shubhashis Sengupta
abstract: Solving large-scale Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problems with Time Windows (CVRPTW) remains challenging because strict operational constraints and scale limit both exact and heuristic methods. We present a hybrid classical-quantum architecture combining Mixed Integer Linear Programming (MILP) with vehicle-level Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO), solved using Toshiba SQBM+ and QAOA on Rigetti Ankaa-3 and IQM Emerald quantum processors. The decomposition avoids the variable growth and constraint-enforcement difficulties of monolithic CVRPTW QUBO formulations. We evaluate the framework on five realistic benchmarks derived from London traffic and location data, spanning 10--70 customers, using a validation pipeline enforcing feasibility and monotone improvement over classical baselines. SQBM+ achieves verified fleet-distance reductions of 2.80% (7,927 m) for the 25-customer instance and 0.22% (1,186 m) for the 55-customer instance. QAOA experiments establish a current hardware boundary for reliable constraint satisfaction at subproblems of up to 4 customers (16 qubits). Diagnostic results identify assignment-level time-window tightness, rather than local route optimization, as the dominant scalability bottleneck. The results demonstrate a practical near-term role for hybrid classical-quantum optimization while establishing empirical limits for current quantum hardware.

infographic.key_insight: A hybrid MILP–QUBO framework delivers verified routing improvements with SQBM+, while QAOA tests identify a current hardware boundary of 4 customers (16 qubits) for reliable constraint satisfaction.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Vehicle-level decomposition offers a practical way to test quantum optimization within routing workflows while validating feasibility and accepting only improvements over classical baselines.
method: Combine classical MILP with vehicle-level QUBO route optimization.
Solve subproblems using Toshiba SQBM+ and QAOA on Rigetti Ankaa-3 and IQM Emerald processors.
Validate operational constraints and require monotone improvement over classical baselines.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across five London-derived benchmarks with 10–70 customers, SQBM+ reduced verified fleet distance by 2.80% (7,927 m) for 25 customers and 0.22% (1,186 m) for 55 customers.
infographic.watch_item: Assignment-level time-window tightness remains the dominant scalability bottleneck, and these results do not establish quantum advantage.
infographic.paper_title: Hybrid Classical-Quantum Optimization for CVRPTW: A Systems Framework with Provable Feasibility and Empirical Hardware Limits

title: QSim-Arena: an evolving developer for quantum simulation advantage
authors: Jue Xu, Yue Wang, Qi Zhao
abstract: Where practical advantage emerges in quantum dynamics simulation remains a central debate in quantum computing. Claimed advantages can be rapidly narrowed or overturned by stronger classical methods, while progress on both sides can outpace the journal publication cycle. We present QSim-Arena, a research framework in which AI agents combine a closed loop of verification and benchmarking with open exploration. Hamiltonians, initial states and accuracy targets for evolved states or observable expectation values provide explicit specifications for evaluating simulation methods. Agents translate published techniques into executable components, reproduce reported results and benchmark their performance across diverse Hamiltonian families. Competing classical methods are implemented and independently crosschecked, providing credible baselines for end-to-end quantum resource estimates based on rigorous error bounds and empirical calibration. Alongside this closed loop, agents recombine classical simulation techniques and co-design fault-tolerant quantum circuits using knowledge extracted from the literature. Initial applications improve baseline resource estimates through the integration of established techniques. QSim-Arena thus treats quantum advantage assessment as an evolving, reproducible research process that can respond to advances in algorithms, error analysis and hardware.

infographic.key_insight: QSim-Arena uses AI agents to make quantum simulation advantage assessment an evolving, reproducible process rather than a fixed comparison.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports more credible quantum resource planning by comparing fault-tolerant designs against independently crosschecked classical baselines.
method: Specify Hamiltonians, initial states and accuracy targets for evolved states or observables.
Translate published methods into executable components, reproduce results and benchmark across Hamiltonian families.
Explore combinations of classical techniques and co-design fault-tolerant quantum circuits using literature-derived knowledge.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports improved baseline resource estimates in initial applications through established techniques, but provides no numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Improved resource estimates do not establish practical quantum advantage; conclusions depend on classical baseline strength and the validity of error bounds and empirical calibration.
infographic.paper_title: QSim-Arena: an evolving developer for quantum simulation advantage

title: Training quantum neural networks one job at a time
authors: Muhammad Faryad, Rabab Alomairy
abstract: When a quantum processor is reached through a cloud queue, a variational algorithm pays for every round trip, and a single round trip can carry many circuits. The classical optimizer therefore decides how much is learned per job, not only per shot. We study this for a quantum neural network classifier. We compare optimizers that are given the same number of jobs and the same shots per job, and that differ only in how they fill each job. This comparison treats hybrid quantum-classical training as an execution-efficiency problem: how to obtain useful optimization progress from each costly interaction with a quantum processor. The resulting perspective connects optimizer design to overhead amortization and efficient use of accelerator resources. A direct port of a batched pattern search that worked for the quantum approximate optimization algorithm stalls once the model has a few dozen parameters. What does transfer is the principle behind it: fill each job with a batch of parameter vectors that is fixed before the job is sent. For circuits built from Pauli rotations the natural batch is the parameter-shift stencil. We show that its gradient error falls as the inverse of the shots per job, while the error of simultaneous-perturbation methods (SPSA) has a floor that no number of shots removes. In simulation, batched parameter-shift training needs between a fifth and a half of the jobs SPSA needs, for 24 to 48 parameters, and the ordering holds at two noise levels. A new structure-aware stencil search reads the same kind of rows as sinusoids and also beats SPSA. On IBM's ibm_fez processor, in three interleaved runs at six and eight qubits, the batched optimizer reached SPSA's final training loss within 4 to 20 of its 50 jobs. Its test accuracy was clearly higher at eight qubits; at six qubits the difference was not significant. All hardware numbers can be re-derived from the raw shots.

infographic.key_insight: Batching parameter-shift evaluations into each quantum job reduces the cloud interactions needed to train a quantum neural network compared with SPSA.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Optimizer design should maximize progress per queued job, not just per shot, to amortize quantum-cloud overhead.
method: Compare optimizers with equal job budgets and shots per job.
Precompute parameter-shift batches for Pauli-rotation circuits.
Test batched training and a structure-aware sinusoidal stencil search against SPSA.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations with 24–48 parameters required 20–50% as many jobs as SPSA; across three interleaved IBM ibm_fez runs at six and eight qubits, batched training matched SPSA’s final loss in 4–20 versus 50 jobs.
infographic.watch_item: Hardware evidence is limited to six and eight qubits, and the test-accuracy advantage was not statistically significant at six qubits.
infographic.paper_title: Training quantum neural networks one job at a time

title: Quantum Material Generation via Coherent Hamiltonian Search
authors: Jiang Yuhan, Matthew Otten
abstract: Discovering new materials with targeted properties is a central goal of materials science, yet the space of candidates is vast. Data-driven generative models learn the distribution of known materials, but they extrapolate poorly, and a generated structure is not known to be stable. A material's properties follow from its Hamiltonian, and a quantum computer can calculate them from it. We introduce the quantum material generative algorithm (QMage), a coherent search, guided by the Hamiltonian, over crystalline configurations of atomic composition, unit cell structure, and atomic positions, for one whose calculated properties meet the targets to within a given error tolerance. The computation is a single coherent quantum circuit in which each configuration's Hamiltonian is block-encoded, its target eigenstate isolated and properties evaluated, and the satisfying configurations amplified by fixed-point search and measured. One framework covers many targets, from formation energy and band gaps to elasticity and conductivity. We design the algorithm for the mature fault-tolerant era and estimate its cost in logical qubits and Toffoli depth from a classically routine benchmark to targets where established methods are unreliable. The approach generates candidate materials from first principles, rather than generalizing from those known, and could enable materials discovery when the target properties are difficult to predict classically.

infographic.key_insight: QMage proposes a coherent quantum search for crystalline materials whose Hamiltonian-derived properties match specified targets within an error tolerance.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could support first-principles materials discovery for properties that established classical methods struggle to predict.
method: Search over atomic compositions, unit cell structures, and atomic positions.
Block-encode each configuration’s Hamiltonian, isolate its target eigenstate, and evaluate material properties.
Amplify configurations meeting the targets using fixed-point search, then measure candidate materials.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports logical-qubit and Toffoli-depth cost estimates spanning a classically routine benchmark and targets where established methods are unreliable, but gives no numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: QMage is designed for mature fault-tolerant quantum computers; practical feasibility depends on the resources required for coherent Hamiltonian encoding and property evaluation.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum Material Generation via Coherent Hamiltonian Search

title: From optimization to construction: Expanding quantum measurement designs
authors: Taotao Zhao, Qianjun Yao, Mengdi Sun, He Li
abstract: Estimating molecular energies on quantum computers requires repeated measurements of many Pauli terms, making sampling a major resource cost. Measurement design chooses which compatible terms are measured together and allocates a finite shot budget among bases to minimize the variance of an energy estimator. We introduce variance-guided measurement group construction (VGMC), which reduces variance beyond optimization on existing measurement bases by changing which Hamiltonian terms share measurement shots. After including every Hamiltonian term measurable in each existing basis, we jointly optimize estimator coefficients and shot allocations to separate inefficient use of these measurements from limitations of their measurement combinations. We compare a candidate's benefit with the cost of withdrawing shots from existing bases, and use the resulting scores to guide greedy construction of qubit-wise commuting groups followed by joint re-optimization. With exact covariances, VGMC outperformed the state-of-the-art measurement design methods across the molecular benchmarks where it introduced additional measurement bases, achieving variance reductions of 18.19%-23.38%. The gains persisted with approximate covariances, and simulations with finite shots indicated lower estimated shot requirements near chemical accuracy. These results show that optimizing how measurements are combined can also guide which terms are measured together, offering a route to reducing the sampling overhead of variational quantum simulation while retaining local measurements on current and near-term devices.

infographic.key_insight: Variance-guided measurement group construction (VGMC) reduces molecular energy estimation variance by redesigning which Pauli terms share measurements, rather than only optimizing existing measurement bases.
infographic.engineering_relevance: VGMC offers a route to lower sampling costs for variational quantum simulations while retaining local measurements compatible with current and near-term devices.
method: Include every Hamiltonian term measurable in each existing basis, then jointly optimize estimator coefficients and shot allocations.
Score candidate groups by their variance benefit relative to the cost of withdrawing shots from existing bases.
Greedily construct qubit-wise commuting groups and jointly re-optimize the expanded measurement design.
infographic.evidence_signal: With exact covariances, VGMC reduced variance by 18.19%–23.38% versus state-of-the-art methods on molecular benchmarks where it added bases; gains persisted with approximate covariances, and finite-shot simulations indicated lower shot requirements near chemical accuracy.
infographic.watch_item: Practical savings depend on covariance estimation quality, and the abstract does not establish hardware-level benefits after accounting for covariance acquisition and classical optimization overhead.
infographic.paper_title: From optimization to construction: Expanding quantum measurement designs

title: Phase Interference and Transverse Catalysts Govern the Noise Fragility of Long-Range Variational Quantum Circuits
authors: Longhui Shen, Fangzhou Jin, Xiaoxia Yi, Bin Guo
abstract: Long-range entangling gates shorten variational state preparation, but they also accelerate operator spreading across the register, linking nonlocality to a presumed noise fragility. Here we show that the single-fault fragility $F$ of a variational circuit is governed by how fault phases interfere on the target Hamiltonian, not by how far faults spread. For Heisenberg chains we prove that two faults with identical extensive support can incur either bounded or extensive energy damage, in the exact ratio $N/2$. A phase-matched longitudinal halo remains energetically dark until ignited by transverse catalysts that break a symmetry of the remote register, namely spatially nonuniform single-qubit rotations or the pair-flip component of two-qubit $XX/YY$ gates, whereas uniform rotations and magnetization-conserving exchange gates leave it strictly dark. In noisy training with full-width long-range $ZZ$ gates, suppressing either catalyst alone leaves circuits trapped on an ignited plateau sustained by remote $XY$ couplings, whereas suppressing both eliminates the plateau, achieves minimal fragility despite larger fault operators, and halves the dephasing error. Training is driven by a race between catalyst pruning and gradient force balance, as annealing the transverse catalysts out of trapped circuits rescues every trajectory while annealing the entire longitudinal sector does not. Combined with the gate-count exposure $λ=pK$, a single fragility measurement accurately predicts the noise-induced energy shift across circuit architectures and noise strengths, reducing ansatz design to a trade-off between coherent expressivity and gate count.

infographic.key_insight: Long-range circuit noise fragility depends on fault-phase interference with the target Hamiltonian, not simply on how far faults spread.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Ansatz design should balance expressivity and gate-count exposure while controlling transverse operations that activate otherwise energetically dark faults.
method: Prove contrasting energy damage from equally extensive faults in Heisenberg chains.
Test catalyst suppression and annealing in noisy training with full-width long-range ZZ gates.
Predict noise-induced energy shifts using single-fault fragility and gate-count exposure λ = pK.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports an exact N/2 damage ratio for equal-support faults, halved dephasing error when both catalysts are suppressed, and rescue of every tested trapped trajectory through catalyst annealing.
infographic.watch_item: Generality beyond the studied Heisenberg-chain circuits and noise settings requires validation.
infographic.paper_title: Phase Interference and Transverse Catalysts Govern the Noise Fragility of Long-Range Variational Quantum Circuits

title: Invariance can prevent overfitting and shortcut learning in Quantum Neural Networks
authors: Giuseppe D'Ambruoso, Giovanni Gramegna, Domenico Pomarico, Giuseppe Magnifico, Cosmo Lupo
abstract: Many image classification tasks have labels that are unchanged by rotations and reflections. Equivariant quantum neural networks incorporate such symmetries by design, but the specific benefit of symmetry is difficult to isolate. Equivariant quantum circuits are usually compared with architectures that also differ in gates, structure or size. Here, we investigate the role of invariance in a controlled setting, classifying images whose labels are invariant under the dihedral group $D_4$. We compare four eight-qubit models with identical encoding, circuit structure and number of trainable parameters, and equivalent dynamical Lie algebras, and benchmark invariant implementations against non-invariant ones in terms of generalization error, robustness to shortcut learning and resilience to a realistic noise model. On four binary tasks, including MNIST and two scientific data sets of galaxies and red blood cells, the invariant models trained on a few tens of images show better generalization than non-invariant ones. Invariance also makes the models immune to orientation shortcuts: when trained with a class-dependent corner watermark, the non-invariant models learn the watermark and often drop to chance level when it is moved. We show that the gain in accuracy of invariant models persists also under a realistic noise model.

infographic.key_insight: Building rotation and reflection invariance into quantum neural networks can reduce overfitting and prevent orientation-based shortcut learning.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For image tasks with symmetry-preserving labels, invariant quantum models can improve generalization from small training sets and retain accuracy gains under realistic simulated noise.
method: Compare four eight-qubit models with identical encoding, circuit structure and parameter counts, and equivalent dynamical Lie algebras.
Evaluate invariant and non-invariant models on image labels unchanged by the dihedral group D4.
Test generalization, class-dependent corner-watermark shortcuts and resilience to a realistic noise model.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across four binary tasks, including MNIST, galaxies and red blood cells, invariant models trained on a few tens of images generalized better, while moving shortcut watermarks often reduced non-invariant models to chance accuracy.
infographic.watch_item: Evidence is limited to eight-qubit models and four binary tasks; benefits depend on the chosen symmetries preserving task labels.
infographic.paper_title: Invariance can prevent overfitting and shortcut learning in Quantum Neural Networks

title: Ensemble phase transitions in measurement-unitary hybrid quantum circuits
authors: Saptarshi Mandal, Sthitadhi Roy
abstract: The universal properties of state ensembles generated by quantum dynamics provide a refined lens into Hilbert-space ergodicity and deep thermalisation, or lack thereof. We investigate deep-ergodicity breaking transitions of an ancillary qubit entangled with a system undergoing dynamics via hybrid quantum circuits, where unitary evolution is interspersed with projective measurements. Specifically, we analyse the statistical properties of two distinct state ensembles: the trajectory ensemble (TE) conditioned on the measurement outcomes of the hybrid circuit, and the projected ensemble (PE) generated by further projective measurements of the system at the final temporal boundary. We find that both ensembles undergo non-analytic changes -- ensemble phase transitions -- at the critical point of the measurement-induced purification transition, despite their first moments remaining completely maximally mixed and blind to the transition. For Haar-random circuits, the TE transitions from a trivial identity ensemble to the uniform Haar ensemble, while the PE transitions from the Haar ensemble to a trivial singleton pure state. In Clifford circuits, absence of non-stabiliserness limits the PE to a $1$-design, while the TE forms a $k$-design for $k \leq 3$. We demonstrate that these genuine ensemble transitions offer a clear physical mechanism for the measurement-induced entanglement or purification transitions, illustrating how the capacity to ergodically steer a quantum subsystem shifts from the temporal boundary measurements in the mixed phase to the bulk trajectory measurements in the pure phase.

infographic.key_insight: Measurement-induced purification coincides with ensemble phase transitions that reveal changes in quantum-state statistics invisible to their maximally mixed first moments.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Ensemble-level diagnostics could help characterize how measurement placement controls quantum-state preparation and ergodicity in hybrid quantum circuits.
method: Study an ancillary qubit entangled with a system undergoing unitary evolution and projective measurements.
Compare trajectory ensembles conditioned on circuit outcomes with projected ensembles formed by final system measurements.
Analyze ensemble transitions in Haar-random and Clifford circuits.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports non-analytic changes in both ensembles at the purification critical point, with distinct Haar-random transitions and Clifford design limits of 1 for projected ensembles and up to 3 for trajectory ensembles.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no quantitative finite-size or hardware-noise evaluation, so practical robustness remains unclear.
infographic.paper_title: Ensemble phase transitions in measurement-unitary hybrid quantum circuits

title: The energetic cost of loading classical data in quantum computers
authors: Joao F. Doriguello, Alessandro Luongo, Harshit Verma
abstract: Quantum algorithms for machine learning, chemistry, and cryptanalysis often assume coherent access to classical data at negligible physical cost. We instead treat data loading as a hardware process and quantify the dynamic energetic cost of a quantum random access memory (QRAM) query on a superconducting processor. Using the metric-noise-resource framework, we relate query fidelity and power to gate duration, relative two-qubit drive strength, and the distribution of attenuation across a multi-stage refrigerator, while accounting for thermal photons and gate errors. We analyze the linear-depth multiplexer and the noise-resilient bucket-brigade architectures, adapting the latter to a native superconducting gate set and refining its fidelity analysis using the fully decomposed gate schedule. For a representative bucket-brigade QRAM query with a $12$-qubit address register we obtain a query fidelity of $0.969$. The query consumes $3.51\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{J}$ of dynamic energy, corresponding to an average dynamic power of $4.38\,\mathrm{W}$ and a peak of $64.4\,\mathrm{W}$. Our optimization shows that, at fixed target fidelity, the operating point and attenuation profile can change the average power by a factor of two or more.

infographic.key_insight: Loading classical data into superconducting quantum computers has a substantial dynamic energy cost that depends on QRAM architecture, control settings, and refrigeration attenuation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: At fixed target fidelity, optimizing operating conditions and attenuation distribution can change average dynamic power by a factor of two or more.
method: Model QRAM fidelity and power using a metric-noise-resource framework that includes thermal photons and gate errors.
Analyze linear-depth multiplexer and bucket-brigade architectures.
Adapt bucket-brigade QRAM to native superconducting gates and evaluate its fully decomposed schedule.
infographic.evidence_signal: For a modeled bucket-brigade query with a 12-qubit address register, the authors report 0.969 fidelity, 3.51×10⁻⁴ J dynamic energy, 4.38 W average dynamic power, and 64.4 W peak dynamic power.
infographic.watch_item: These model-based dynamic-cost estimates do not establish experimentally measured performance or total system energy consumption.
infographic.paper_title: The energetic cost of loading classical data in quantum computers

title: Uncertainty-aware quantum machine learning based on Dempster-Shafer theory
authors: Marie Kempkes, Jakob Spiegelberg, Evert van Nieuwenburg, Vedran Dunjko
abstract: A large body of work in quantum machine learning has centered on characterizing the expressivity and performance of quantum models. In contrast, little attention has been paid to the reliability of predictions beyond average performance measures such as accuracy. In this work, we introduce an uncertainty-aware quantum classification framework based on Dempster-Shafer theory. This theory allows to express uncertainty through weights assigned not only to individual classification labels but to sets of labels. We introduce a training strategy that enables parameterized quantum circuits to learn such assignments directly from data. This provides an efficient way to prepare the corresponding quantum states and enables the application of different post-processing strategies. In particular, it offers a practical setting for quantum Dempster-Shafer fusion procedures with polynomial resource requirements, even when the corresponding mass functions are defined over exponentially many subsets. Overall, our work represents a step toward enabling quantum models to express uncertainty about their predictions, thereby extending the evaluation of quantum models beyond predictive performance alone.

infographic.key_insight: Quantum classifiers can express uncertainty by assigning belief to sets of labels rather than only individual labels.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports uncertainty-aware quantum predictions and quantum evidence fusion with polynomial resource requirements, even for mass functions over exponentially many subsets.
method: Represent predictive uncertainty using Dempster–Shafer mass assignments over label sets.
Train parameterized quantum circuits to learn these assignments directly from data.
Prepare corresponding quantum states for uncertainty post-processing and evidence fusion.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes a training framework and resource-efficiency claims but reports no datasets, numerical benchmarks, or uncertainty-quality metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Practical uncertainty quality and hardware costs require validation beyond the stated polynomial resource scaling.
infographic.paper_title: Uncertainty-aware quantum machine learning based on Dempster-Shafer theory

title: Noise-Protected Superconducting Qudits from Higher-Harmonic Josephson Junctions
authors: Hamed Vakili
abstract: Qudits, which generalize qubits to $d$ levels, store more information per circuit element than qubits. As with qubits, however, their sensitivity to noise must be overcome before they can be used for fault-tolerant quantum computing. Here we show that, by exploiting the second harmonic of the current--phase relation, a superconducting loop of three Josephson junctions can host qutrits strongly protected against relaxation, while dephasing limits their coherence. When the second harmonic is positive, a simple loop with a small asymmetry between the junctions provides a tunable, symmetry-protected qutrit. When it is negative, a protected qutrit can be realized by adding a small symmetry-breaking term, such as a weak Josephson diode effect. The two designs involve different trade-offs: the first has an exact charge selection rule, whereas the second is nearly insensitive to charge noise and its quasiparticle errors can be corrected. The preferable choice therefore depends on the materials used. Both require a sizable second harmonic to begin with, and we identify altermagnetic Josephson junctions as a candidate platform. Finally, microscopic calculations show that a gate voltage selects the sign of the second harmonic in these junctions, although gate-voltage noise then becomes the leading source of dephasing. These findings establish the sign of the second harmonic as a design principle for protected superconducting qudits.

infographic.key_insight: The sign of a sizable second harmonic in a Josephson junction’s current–phase relation enables distinct superconducting qutrit designs strongly protected against relaxation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Three-junction loops could encode three-level quantum information with protection tailored to material-dependent charge-noise and quasiparticle constraints.
method: Use a positive second harmonic and slight junction asymmetry for a tunable qutrit with an exact charge selection rule.
Use a negative second harmonic and weak symmetry breaking for near charge-noise insensitivity and correctable quasiparticle errors.
Calculate how gate voltage selects the harmonic sign in candidate altermagnetic Josephson junctions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical protection mechanisms and microscopic gate-tuning calculations, but no experimental coherence measurements.
infographic.watch_item: Both designs require a sizable second harmonic; dephasing remains limiting, with gate-voltage noise leading in the gate-tuned platform.
infographic.paper_title: Noise-Protected Superconducting Qudits from Higher-Harmonic Josephson Junctions

title: Scalable Compilation of Resource-Efficient Tapers for High-Confidence Quantum Phase Estimation
authors: David Raveh, Andrew Sornborger, Yiğit Subaşı, Lukasz Cincio
abstract: Quantum phase estimation is a key component of many quantum algorithms. Recently, high-confidence, tapered QPE (tQPE) has been introduced, significantly reducing the number of ancilla qubits necessary for a given failure probability, $ε$. We consider tQPE with $p = l+m$ ancillas, where $l$ represents the number of ancillas necessary to estimate a phase to a given resolution and $m$ represents the number of ''confidence'' qubits added to ensure a desired success probability. With tQPE the failure probability decays double exponentially in $m$, implying that only a few confidence qubits suffice for virtually any problem of interest. A key challenge for tQPE is the construction of the quantum circuit for preparing the taper state on the ancilla register. Here, we develop scalable tensor network methods (previous work was limited to ($l + m = 24$)) giving highly optimized state preparation circuits for optimally concentrated DPSS (Slepian) tapers. We provide an accompanying database of resource-efficient state preparation circuits for $l = 1, \dots, 50$ and $m = 1, \dots, 4$. Our circuits are shallow enough for a demonstration on near-term devices for small values of $l$. We run tQPE circuits for a 1-qubit system initialized in the ground state on Quantinuum's H2-2 quantum computer, demonstrating a $3\times$ to $18\times$ reduction in failure probability for $l=1,\ldots,10$ on a noisy device.

infographic.key_insight: Scalable compilation of optimized taper states makes high-confidence quantum phase estimation practical with fewer ancilla qubits.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Resource-efficient taper preparation can reduce ancilla overhead while keeping small phase-estimation circuits shallow enough for near-term hardware demonstrations.
method: Use tapered QPE with resolution qubits plus a few confidence qubits, yielding failure probability that decays double exponentially with confidence-qubit count.
Compile optimally concentrated DPSS (Slepian) taper states using scalable tensor-network methods.
Provide a circuit database spanning 1–50 resolution qubits and 1–4 confidence qubits.
infographic.evidence_signal: On Quantinuum H2-2, tQPE experiments with a one-qubit system initialized in its ground state demonstrated 3×–18× lower failure probability for 1–10 resolution qubits.
infographic.watch_item: Hardware validation covers a one-qubit system and small registers; performance for larger systems and compiled tapers remains to be demonstrated.
infographic.paper_title: Scalable Compilation of Resource-Efficient Tapers for High-Confidence Quantum Phase Estimation

title: Scalable Pauli propagation through $\mathbb{F}_2$-linear partitioning
authors: Alev Orfi, Andrew Kille, J. Clayton Peacock, Jack Dunham, Lukas Devos
abstract: Pauli propagation simulates quantum circuits and many-body dynamics by evolving observables in the Heisenberg picture as sparse sums of Pauli strings. As Pauli-string operations reduce to bit manipulations, its performance is limited by memory bandwidth and capacity rather than computational throughput. Pooling the memory of many cores and nodes is hindered by the deduplication step after every gate, which can require global synchronization. We avoid this bottleneck by partitioning the strings with an $\mathbb{F}_2$-linear hash function, which guarantees that a $k$-qubit channel couples each partition to at most $4^k$ partitions fixed by the gate, decomposing gate application into independent tasks with bounded communication. Benchmarks of our open-source implementation demonstrate efficient parallel scaling within and across compute nodes, enabling simulations with over $10^{11}$ Pauli strings and extending the accessible timescales of quantum many-body dynamics.

infographic.key_insight: An F₂-linear hash partitions Pauli strings so a k-qubit channel couples each partition to at most 4^k gate-determined partitions, avoiding global deduplication synchronization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Bounded communication helps pool memory across cores and compute nodes for larger classical simulations of quantum circuits and many-body dynamics.
method: Evolve observables as sparse sums of Pauli strings in the Heisenberg picture.
Partition strings using an F₂-linear hash function.
Apply gates through independent tasks with bounded interpartition communication.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports efficient parallel scaling within and across nodes, simulations exceeding 10^11 Pauli strings, and access to longer many-body dynamics timescales using an open-source implementation.
infographic.watch_item: Memory bandwidth and capacity remain constraints, while the 4^k communication bound grows exponentially with channel locality.
infographic.paper_title: Scalable Pauli propagation through $\mathbb{F}_2$-linear partitioning

title: Normalizing Flows for Classical Simulation of Quantum Circuits in Phase Space
authors: Edward Jiang, Timothy Heightman, Marcin Płodzień
abstract: We present a novel framework to learn a representation of quantum circuits based on the phase space formulation of many-body systems. Given that $N$-qubit states can be represented as probability distributions on a smooth $2N$-dimensional manifold, we show how unitary gates can be parameterized as normalizing flows between these distributions, opening a new avenue for quantum circuit simulation using generative models. We evaluate our method on three common families of quantum circuits, and show that its accuracy exceeds that of current state-of-the-art neural network methods for large system sizes.

infographic.key_insight: Normalizing flows can model quantum gates as transformations between phase-space probability distributions, enabling a generative approach to classical quantum circuit simulation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a potential alternative to neural-network quantum simulators when accuracy at larger qubit counts is important.
method: Represent N-qubit states as probability distributions on a smooth 2N-dimensional manifold.
Parameterize unitary gates as normalizing flows between these distributions.
Learn phase-space representations for quantum circuit simulation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports evaluation on three common circuit families and higher accuracy than current state-of-the-art neural-network methods at large system sizes.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify runtime, memory use, or training costs, so practical scaling advantages remain unclear.
infographic.paper_title: Normalizing Flows for Classical Simulation of Quantum Circuits in Phase Space
